---
title: "Python answer tests and custom checkers"
---

Use a Python checker when the task accepts a mathematical property rather
than one displayed answer. Install CTM Assessment and use
`filters: [ctm-assessment]`; the shared checker library supplies Python and
SymPy. Checker source is trusted author code and is public in the static
page. Keep credentials and private data out of it.

## Choose the mathematical test

Use the XML's ordinary answer tests for equivalence, written form and numeric
tolerance. For matrix properties, `PythonChecker` nodes can select these
predicates from `ctm_checkers.matrix`:

| Name | Options | What the node checks |
|---|---|---|
| `basis` | `space: nullspace`, `columnspace` or `rowspace` | A basis for the space of the matrix in `<tans>` |
| `matrix_property` | `property: integer_entries`, `determinant` or `identity` | The indicated property equals `<tans>` |
| `is_hermitian` | None | Hermitian symmetry equals the boolean `<tans>` |
| `is_positive_definite` | None | Positivity of the Hermitian part equals `<tans>` |
| `is_hpd` | None | Hermitian symmetry and positive definiteness together |

For example, a basis node uses:

```xml
<answertest>PythonChecker</answertest>
<sans>ans</sans>
<tans>A</tans>
<testoptions>{"checker":"basis","options":{"space":"nullspace"}}</testoptions>
```

`A` is the defining matrix, not a displayed basis. The basis predicate accepts
any independent family that spans the required space. It reports green,
red and dependent-vector assessments without preferring an ordering. Library
predicates keep their exact rational-domain and matrix-size restrictions.
A question using them needs no checker filename or block `checker:`.

## Symmetric positive definite matrices

For a real matrix, `is_hpd` requires symmetry and positive definiteness.
For a complex matrix, it requires Hermitian symmetry and positive
definiteness. The library checks every leading principal minor; a positive
determinant alone is insufficient. Use integers or exact fractions for real
and imaginary parts and `%i` for the imaginary unit.

```{.stack-question #docs-spd-matrix}
#| label: docs-spd-matrix
#| file: ../questions/symmetric-positive-definite.xml
#| question: A positive definite matrix
#| review: true
```

Separate `is_hermitian` and `is_positive_definite` response trees can award
separate marks. A nonsymmetric matrix can pass the latter because it checks
the Hermitian part; `is_hpd` requires both conditions. See the
[separate-mark example](../examples.qmd#symmetry-and-positive-definiteness-separately).

Try the same matrix with separate marks for symmetry and positivity:

```{.stack-question #docs-spd-separate}
#| label: docs-spd-separate
#| file: ../questions/symmetric-positive-definite-prt.xml
#| question: Hermitian symmetry and positive definiteness separately
#| review: true
```

## PythonChecker API and a scalar example

Write a block `checker:` with `check(response, symbols)`. The same function
contract works in math-exercise when its field labels equal the STACK input
names. This example accepts any positive integer multiple of the displayed
number:

```{.stack-question #docs-custom-multiple}
#| label: docs-custom-multiple
#| variants: 3
#| file: ../questions/python-checker.xml
#| question: A positive integer multiple (PythonChecker)
#| checker: |
#|   def check(response, symbols):
#|       answer = response["answers"]["ans"]
#|       divisor = response["variables"]["d"]
#|       if answer.is_Integer is not True:
#|           return {"valid": False, "feedback": "Enter an integer value."}
#|       correct = answer > 0 and answer % divisor == 0
#|       return {"correct": bool(correct),
#|               "feedback": "" if correct else "Use a positive integer multiple of the given number."}
#| tests:
#|   - name: displayed multiple
#|     answers: {ans: d}
#|     expect: correct
#|   - name: wrong offset
#|     answers: {ans: d+1}
#|     expect: wrong
#|   - name: fractional input
#|     answers: {ans: 'raw("1/2")'}
#|     expect: invalid
#| review: true
```

The XML node uses `{"checker":"check"}`. It adds its own evaluated values as
`response["node"] = {"sans": ..., "tans": ..., "options": ...}`. `options`
is the literal JSON object inside `testoptions`, never evaluated as CAS or
Python. A partial checker result takes the node's false branch; the node's
normal branch scores still determine that XML tree's score.

## Response and result

The checker receives these values after the selected backend has validated
all inputs:

| Key | Value |
|---|---|
| `kind` | `"expressions"` |
| `raw` | Student strings in XML input order |
| `expressions` | Parsed values in the same order |
| `answers` | Parsed values keyed by XML input name |
| `teacher` | Teacher values keyed by XML input name |
| `variables` | Exact question variables |
| `inputs` | Named input descriptions, including `raw` and `canonical` |
| `variant` | `{n, id, hash}`; an unapproved candidate has no published number |
| `node` | Present only during a `PythonChecker` node call |

Matrix input descriptions also carry `rows`, `cols`, flattened `expressions`
and a SymPy `matrix`. `symbols` maps free symbol names to their SymPy symbols,
with the question's assumptions. The checker namespace contains the shared
math-exercise helpers, including SymPy names and `assess_basis`.

Return `True` or `False`, a number between 0 and 1, or a dictionary containing
`score` or `correct`. Optional keys are `feedback`, `show_score` and
`assessment`. Feedback is plain text. A matrix assessment names the input:

```python
return {"score": 0.5, "feedback": "Review the dependent columns.",
        "assessment": {"ans": {"columns": ["correct", "dependent"]}}}
```

Each assessment list must match the submitted row or column count. A result
such as `{"valid": False, "feedback": "Enter an integer value."}` rejects the
attempt without a score. Invalid attempts clear vector assessments. A checker
that raises, returns a malformed result or cannot decode a required author
value is an author error; it does not count as a wrong learner answer.
Each invocation gets a fresh namespace.

## Score and placement

A block checker creates an implicit response tree named `checker`, with
`checker-value: 1` by default. Its normalized score counts alongside the
XML trees:

$$
\text{score}=\frac{\sum_{\text{trees}}\text{value}\times\text{score}}
                       {\sum_{\text{trees}}\text{value}}.
$$

For XML tree scores 1 and 0, both of weight 1, and a checker score 0.5 with
`checker-value: 2`, the question scores 0.5. With no XML trees, the checker
supplies the whole grade. Use `[[feedback:checker]]` in CASText to place its
feedback. Penalties and score rounding follow the same rules as XML trees.
The name `checker` is reserved when the block defines a checker.

The XML node and the implicit checker are separate evaluations. A node calls
the function as a predicate and supplies `response["node"]`; the implicit
checker call has no `node` key and contributes its numeric score. Write the
function to support both contexts when the XML calls it.

## Test and publish

[Run XML and declarative question tests](python-answer-tests.qmd) for every
variant, inspect the student previews, and approve the variants before
publishing. Review mode permits proposals for teacher inspection; it does not
approve them. Normal publishing requires current approved variants.

The old `python-checkers:` filename, `CHECKERS` registry and
`ctm_checkers.stack.checker_api` module have been removed. Move custom logic
into `checker:` and change its arguments to `response, symbols`. Supplied
matrix predicates now come from the shared library without a filename.
Both backends implement this contract. Maxima calls the same checker with
validated written values, while native Maxima owns question preparation and
compiled response-tree routing. See the [native guide](native-authoring.qmd).
